questions.stem: What does Erikson's theory of psychosocial development describe?
options: Eight stages from infancy to late adulthood, each centred on a conflict between two outcomes
Four stages from birth to adolescence, each defined by a new way of thinking logically
Learning that happens when a more skilled person guides a child just beyond their current ability
Attachment bonds that form in infancy and act as a model for later relationships
questions.explanation: Erikson proposed eight psychosocial stages spanning the whole lifespan, each with a crisis such as trust versus mistrust. Four stages ending in adolescence describes Piaget's cognitive theory, and guided learning describes Vygotsky.

questions.stem: Baby Ari's carers respond warmly and reliably whenever he cries. According to Erikson, which outcome is this most likely to support?
options: Autonomy, in the stage of autonomy versus shame and doubt
Initiative, in the stage of initiative versus guilt
Intimacy, in the stage of intimacy versus isolation
Trust, in the stage of trust versus mistrust
questions.explanation: Erikson's first stage, in infancy, is trust versus mistrust. Consistent, responsive care leads the infant to see the world as safe and people as dependable.

questions.stem: Two-year-old Mia insists on choosing her clothes and dressing herself, and her parents let her try. Which of Erikson's crises is she working through?
options: Initiative versus guilt
Industry versus inferiority
Trust versus mistrust
Autonomy versus shame and doubt
questions.explanation: In early childhood the crisis is autonomy versus shame and doubt: toddlers want to do things for themselves. Being allowed to try builds autonomy, while harsh criticism of failures can lead to shame and doubt.

questions.stem: Four-year-old Sam loves inventing games and organising his friends, but his carer often scolds him for making a mess. According to Erikson, what might Sam develop?
options: A sense of inferiority about his schoolwork
A sense of role confusion about who he is
A sense of guilt about taking initiative
A sense of mistrust towards other people
questions.explanation: The preschool crisis is initiative versus guilt. Children who are discouraged or punished for planning and starting activities may come to feel guilty about taking initiative.

questions.stem: Twenty-six-year-old Priya is working on forming a close, committed relationship with a partner. Which of Erikson's stages is she in?
options: Generativity versus stagnation
Integrity versus despair
Intimacy versus isolation
Identity versus role confusion
questions.explanation: In young adulthood the crisis is intimacy versus isolation: forming deep, committed relationships. Identity versus role confusion comes before it, in adolescence.

questions.stem: Fifty-year-old Tom spends weekends coaching junior football and mentoring young staff at work. According to Erikson, which outcome is he achieving?
options: Integrity, by accepting the life he has lived
Industry, by mastering new skills and comparing himself with others
Intimacy, by forming close and committed relationships
Generativity, by contributing to the next generation
questions.explanation: Middle adulthood's crisis is generativity versus stagnation, and generativity means caring for and contributing to younger people and society. Integrity versus despair is the final stage, a review of one's whole life.

questions.stem: How did Erikson view a crisis that was not successfully resolved at its usual stage?
options: It had no effect on later stages, because each stage is completely independent
It always caused a psychological disorder in adulthood that later needed treatment
It could affect later development, but could still be worked through later in life
It fixed the person's development permanently, so later stages could not begin
questions.explanation: Erikson saw each stage as building on the ones before, so an unresolved crisis can make later ones harder. He did not see this as permanent; the conflict can be revisited and resolved later.

questions.stem: How does Erikson's theory differ from Piaget's?
options: Erikson rejects the idea that development happens in a series of stages
Erikson explains development entirely by genetic maturation
Erikson focuses on social and emotional development across the whole lifespan
Erikson focuses on cognitive development, in four stages that end with adolescence
questions.explanation: Piaget described cognitive development in four stages ending in adolescence. Erikson described psychosocial development, shaped by relationships and society, in eight stages through to late adulthood.

questions.stem: Erikson's and Piaget's theories both describe development as a series of distinct stages. What view of development does this reflect?
options: Reversible development, with people moving freely between stages
Discontinuous development, with qualitative changes from stage to stage
Continuous development, with small gradual changes adding up over time
Nature-only development, with no influence from the environment
questions.explanation: Stage theories treat development as discontinuous: each stage is qualitatively different from the last. A continuous view sees development as a gradual, steady build-up of the same abilities.

questions.stem: What is a longitudinal study in lifespan psychology?
options: One that compares identical twins with non-identical twins
One that studies one person in great depth at a single time
One that follows the same group of people over an extended period
One that compares groups of different ages at a single point in time
questions.explanation: A longitudinal study tracks the same participants as they age, so it can observe change within individuals. Comparing different age groups at one time is a cross-sectional design.

questions.stem: Growing Up in Australia, the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, follows about 10 000 children and families. What is a key strength of this design?
options: It controls the children's environments to test cause and effect
It shows how the same individuals change as they grow up
It produces results quickly because each child is tested only once
It removes the chance of participants dropping out over the years
questions.explanation: Following the same children over many years shows individual developmental change and avoids differences between generations. Longitudinal studies are slow and do lose participants over time (attrition).

questions.stem: A researcher wants results within a few months on how memory differs between 20-, 50- and 80-year-olds. Which design is most practical?
options: Cross-sectional
Longitudinal
Case study
Twin study
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional study can compare the three age groups at one time, giving results quickly and cheaply. A longitudinal study would need to follow people for about sixty years.

questions.stem: A cross-sectional study finds that 70-year-olds use social media much less than 20-year-olds. Why should the researchers not conclude that ageing reduces social media use?
options: Cross-sectional studies can only collect qualitative data, not numbers
The same participants were tested repeatedly, so practice effects changed their answers
The groups grew up in different eras, so the gap may reflect experience, not age
The groups are too similar in age for any real difference to be found
questions.explanation: Different age groups belong to different generations (cohorts) with different experiences, such as growing up with or without the internet. A cross-sectional design cannot separate these cohort effects from the effects of ageing.

questions.stem: Which is a common limitation of longitudinal studies?
options: Each participant is studied only once, so change cannot be seen
They cannot be used to study children, only adults
Participants drop out over time, which can bias the remaining sample
Differences found may be due to the groups growing up in different eras
questions.explanation: Over many years participants move, lose interest or die, and those who remain may differ from those who left (attrition). Cohort differences are a limitation of cross-sectional designs instead.

questions.stem: What proportion of their genes do identical (monozygotic) and non-identical (dizygotic) twins share?
options: Both types share about 100% of their genes
Identical about 100%, non-identical about 50% on average
Identical about 50%, non-identical about 25% on average
Identical about 100%, non-identical about 25% on average
questions.explanation: Identical twins develop from one fertilised egg, so they share nearly all their genes. Non-identical twins come from two eggs and share about half on average, like other siblings.

questions.stem: For a trait, concordance is 0.80 for identical twins and 0.40 for non-identical twins raised together. What does this suggest?
options: The trait is caused entirely by the environment the twins share
The trait is unrelated to either genes or the environment
Genes contribute to the trait, but the environment also plays a part
The trait is caused entirely by genes, with no environmental influence
questions.explanation: Identical twins, who share more genes, are more alike than non-identical twins, which points to a genetic contribution. Because identical twins are not 100% concordant, non-genetic factors must matter too.

questions.stem: In an adoption study, adopted children resemble their biological parents more than their adoptive parents on a trait. What does this suggest?
options: Heredity (nature) has an important influence on the trait
The family environment (nurture) is the main influence on the trait
The trait develops only after children leave the family home
The trait is caused by the adoption itself
questions.explanation: Adopted children share genes with their biological parents but their environment with their adoptive parents. Greater resemblance to biological parents therefore points to heredity.

questions.stem: A lifespan study asks older adults to describe, in their own words, how retirement changed their sense of purpose. What kind of data does this produce?
options: Cross-sectional data
Physiological data
Qualitative data
Quantitative data
questions.explanation: Descriptions in participants' own words are qualitative data, rich in meaning but harder to compare. Scores, ratings or counts would be quantitative. Cross-sectional describes a design, not a type of data.

questions.stem: Researchers plan a study of six-year-old children's friendships. Which ethical step is essential?
options: Keeping the children in the study even if they want to stop
Obtaining informed consent from a parent or guardian
Telling the children's teachers each child's individual results
Using the children's real names in the published report
questions.explanation: Children cannot give full informed consent, so a parent or guardian must, and the child should still agree and be free to withdraw. Results must be kept confidential, not shared or published with names.

questions.stem: In a past study, identical siblings were deliberately placed in separate adoptive families and studied for years without the families being told they had a twin or triplet. Which ethical principles did this breach?
options: Debriefing only, since consent is not needed for observation
Confidentiality only, since the results were never published
Informed consent and avoiding deception and harm
Random allocation and the use of a control group
questions.explanation: The families never agreed to the separation or the research and were deceived about it, and the separation could cause lasting harm. Random allocation and control groups are features of research design, not ethical principles.

questions.stem: What is ethnocentrism?
options: Valuing every culture equally and studying each on its own terms
Preferring the culture of another country over the culture of one's own
Belonging to several cultural groups at the same time
Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own culture
questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism means treating one's own culture as the standard for judging others. Considering each culture on its own terms is cultural relativism.

questions.stem: Why might established theories of lifespan development not apply equally to all people?
options: They were tested on so many cultures that they describe no group well
They were developed using only non-human primates rather than people
They were designed to describe adults only, not children
They were based mostly on research with participants in Western countries
questions.explanation: Much of the research behind these theories was done in Western countries, so their idea of normal development reflects Western values. They may not transfer to non-Western cultures.

questions.stem: A theory treats early independence from family as the healthy outcome of childhood. In a culture that values interdependence, children are expected to stay closely tied to family. What risk does applying the theory there carry?
options: The theory would become more accurate because it is tested on another culture
The children would change their behaviour to fit the theory's stages
Typical development in that culture could be wrongly judged as delayed or unhealthy
Children in that culture would be judged as developing much faster than they really are
questions.explanation: This is ethnocentrism: using one culture's values as the yardstick. Behaviour that is normal and valued in an interdependent culture could be misread as a problem.

questions.stem: A teenager who migrated to Australia moves between her family's culture at home and Australian culture at school. Why might an ethnocentric theory of identity fit her poorly?
options: It applies only to people who have never moved to a different country
It describes cognitive development, so it says nothing about identity
It assumes one cultural path to identity, not one formed across two cultures
It assumes identity is fixed at birth and so cannot change during adolescence at all
questions.explanation: Theories built on one culture's experience may not capture people of migrant or multicultural backgrounds, whose identity draws on more than one set of values and expectations.

questions.stem: Which is a positive impact of online technology on adolescents' development?
options: Isolated young people can find supportive communities and make connections
Constant comparison with edited images of peers can lower self-esteem
Time spent online can replace face-to-face practice of conversational skills
Online bullying can follow young people home and continue at any hour
questions.explanation: Online connection can help adolescents who are isolated, for example by distance or illness, to find peers and support. The other options are negative impacts.

questions.stem: Fifteen-year-old Zoe carefully chooses which photos to post so that her friends see her as confident and popular. What is this an example of?
options: Impression management
Cyberbullying
Digital privacy
Fake news
questions.explanation: Impression management is controlling how others see you, and social media makes it easy to curate a self-image. This links to Erikson's adolescent task of forming an identity.

questions.stem: Why might heavy use of socially rewarding online technology hold back some children's development?
options: Time online can displace practice of skills like face-to-face talk and physical play
Online technology cannot be used to practise any spoken language or literacy skills
Using screens permanently stops the brain's motor areas from developing
Children who use technology cannot later develop social relationships
questions.explanation: The more time spent online, the less time there may be for practising verbal communication and motor skills in person. Technology can also support literacy and language, so blanket claims that it causes permanent damage go too far.

questions.stem: How can online technology support older people, including those with dementia?
options: Technology can cure dementia by regrowing the neurons damaged by the disease
Online games prevent all age-related decline in memory, attention and motor skills
Technology cannot help them, because older people are unable to learn new skills
Apps and devices can provide memory prompts and exercises that help maintain skills
questions.explanation: Reminders, memory exercises and video contact can help older people maintain knowledge, skills and connection. Technology does not cure dementia or prevent all decline.

questions.stem: A twelve-year-old shares a dramatic news story online without checking it, and it turns out to be false. Which skill does this suggest they need to develop?
options: Secure attachment, including trust in a consistent caregiver
Digital literacy, including checking the source and accuracy of information
Motor skills, including faster typing and more accurate use of a mouse or touchscreen
Concrete operational thinking, including conservation of number and volume
questions.explanation: Constant online news and fake news make it important for young people to learn to evaluate sources. This is part of the digital and literacy skills affected by online technology.
